title: Counterplay to a scaled technique is one of three things
summary: Counterplay to any scaled technique is always exceeding its Frontage, outlasting its Sustain, or shortening its Re-form (via drill, veterancy, redundant command, or a counter-Domain).
verbatim: The counterplay to any scaled technique is therefore always one of three things: 1. Exceed its Frontage so the war continues where it is not. 2. Outlast its Sustain so the practitioner pays and gains nothing. 3. Shorten its Re-form, which is what drill, veterancy, redundant command and a counter-Domain seated toward your own men are all purchased to do.

title: Frontage — how much line a technique affects
summary: Frontage is how much line a technique affects, in men or paces; the distinction between a personal weapon and an instrument of war is width, not power, and most spectacular techniques are narrow.
verbatim: Frontage. How much line the technique affects, in men or in paces. A frontage of twelve men is a personal weapon used in a battle. A frontage of three hundred is an instrument of war. The distinction is width, not power, and most spectacular techniques are narrow.

title: Re-form — whether and how fast a formation recovers cohesion
summary: Re-form is how long an affected formation needs to recover cohesion, and whether it recovers at all — the field that decides engagements and the one authors most often fail to decide before writing.
verbatim: Re-form. How long an affected formation needs to recover cohesion, and whether it recovers at all. This is the field that decides engagements and the one authors most often fail to decide before writing. A technique that breaks a line for ten minutes has bought a local advantage. One that breaks a line permanently has ended the war on that flank.

title: Sustain — how long, and at what cost to the practitioner
summary: Sustain is how long an effect holds before Essence cost forces cessation, and what the practitioner cannot do while holding it — the load-bearing clause, since it tells you what the enemy is free to do during the window.
verbatim: Sustain. How long the effect can be held before Essence cost forces cessation, and what the practitioner cannot do while holding it. The second clause is the load-bearing one, because it tells you what the enemy is free to do during the window and therefore where the scene's real tension sits.

title: Frontage, Sustain and Re-form are mandatory at scale
summary: Three further fields (Frontage, Sustain, Re-form) are mandatory for any technique deployed against a formation; a technique that cannot be given all three does not belong on a battlefield.
verbatim: Three further fields are mandatory for any technique deployed against a formation. A technique that cannot be given all three does not belong on a battlefield and should not be written into one.
notes: This is the origin Pack Two's Amendment Six.7 explicitly says it restates (R2-6-FRONTAGE_SUSTAIN_REFORM).

title: Interior action of a battle occurs in its aftermath
summary: Whatever an engagement will do to characters' relationships happens in the three days afterward, over the burial detail and the arguments about who should have done what — the fight itself is too loud and too fast for anyone to change during it.
verbatim: Rule: the interior action of a battle occurs in its aftermath. Whatever the engagement was going to do to your characters' relationships, it does in the three days afterward, over the burial detail, in the sick lines, and in the arguments about who should have done what. The fight itself is too loud and too fast for anyone to change during it.
notes: This is the founding principle Pack Two's entire "Interior Action at Scale" amendment (the Single Act, R2-5-SINGLE_ACT_RULE) builds a concrete method for.

title: The five-stage aftermath sequence, touch at least two
summary: Per the Mass Combat Craft Guide §7: the wounded left where they fell, the stripping, the late and cursory burial, the disease, and the district that does not recover in the season — any aftermath scene should touch at least two.
verbatim: The five-stage aftermath sequence (per the Mass Combat Craft Guide section 7): the wounded left where they fell, the stripping, the late and cursory burial, the disease, and the district that does not recover in the season. Any aftermath scene should touch at least two.

title: In mass combat, name three characters carry interiority
summary: The one-italic-thought-per-NPC standard is suspended in mass combat; no more than three characters carry interiority through a battle sequence, everyone else is exterior only, and interiority for named characters outside the three is deferred to the aftermath.
verbatim: The one-private-italic-thought-per-named-NPC standard is suspended in mass combat. It exists to make a small cast feel populated and it does the opposite at scale, producing a scene that reads as a poll of forty consciousnesses. Replacement standard: name three. No more than three characters carry interiority through a battle sequence. Everyone else is exterior only: actions, voices, bodies. Interiority for named characters outside the three is deferred to the aftermath, where it lands harder because the reader has been waiting for it.

title: Plan the aftermath first, the engagement second
summary: When planning a battle scene, plan the aftermath first; the engagement exists to produce the conditions of the aftermath. If you cannot state what the aftermath scene is for before writing the battle, the battle has no reason to be in the book.
verbatim: Structural consequence: when planning a battle scene, plan the aftermath first and the engagement second. The engagement exists to produce the conditions of the aftermath. If you cannot state what the aftermath scene is for before you write the battle, the battle has no reason to be in the book.

title: The Scene Standards, and their mass-combat exception
summary: The standing Scene Standards (minimum 2,500 words, layered sensory opening, one private italic thought per named NPC, no section spacers, end on physical action) apply in full to all scenes except mass combat sequences, where two provisions are amended.
verbatim: The standing Scene Standards (minimum 2,500 words, layered sensory opening, one private italic thought per named NPC, no section spacers, end on physical action) apply in full to all scenes except mass combat sequences, where two provisions are amended.
notes: Checked against R12-8-SCENE_STANDARDS_BANS_STRUCK (Pack Twelve §8): that row strikes "sentence-level bans on mechanism explanation and metaphysical numbers" from "Scene Standards," but this row's five listed items (word count, sensory opening, italic thought, no section spacers, physical-action close) contain no such bans. Either "Scene Standards" grew additional mechanism/number bans somewhere between Pack One and Pack Twelve that this corpus doesn't otherwise capture, or Pack Twelve means a different document by the same name. Left unresolved; no supersedes link asserted in either direction.

title: The word floor covers the engagement plus its aftermath
summary: The 2,500-word minimum applies to the engagement plus its aftermath treated as one unit, not the fighting alone; a battle that ends when the fighting ends has not met the standard regardless of length.
verbatim: The 2,500-word minimum applies to the engagement plus its aftermath treated as one unit, not to the fighting alone. A battle sequence that ends when the fighting ends has not met the standard regardless of its length.

title: Mass Combat Guide takes precedence once a formation exists
summary: The Combat Craft Guide governs duels and small actions; the Mass Combat Craft Guide takes precedence the moment a formation exists, and duel instruments (the three-layer hit model, HEMA vocabulary, armour-tier breakdown) are suspended or replaced accordingly.
verbatim: Precedence. This guide governs duels and small actions. The Mass Combat Craft Guide takes precedence the moment a formation exists. The three-layer hit model, the HEMA vocabulary and the armour-tier breakdown are all duel instruments and are explicitly suspended or replaced in mass combat per that guide's sections 1, 3 and 4.
notes: This is the precedence relationship Pack Eleven's R11-3-DUAL_ANSWER_SILHOUETTE cites when confirming "the Combat Craft Guide survives intact."

title: Cozbi's grammar deferred, deserves a proper pass
summary: Cozbi's grammar is deferred deliberately; her combat material is extensive and deserves a proper pass rather than a guess.
verbatim: Cozbi's grammar. Deferred deliberately. Her combat material is extensive and deserves a proper pass rather than a guess.
notes: The origin statement of this docket item (restated in Packs Two and Three); closed by Pack Three's Expenditure assignment (R3-7-COZBI_ASSIGNED). Marked superseded for docket cleanliness, same basis as R2-OP-COZBI_GRAMMAR.

title: No standard exists for naval, siege or cavalry prose
summary: No standard exists for naval, siege or cavalry prose, flagged in the Mass Combat Guide's own open gaps.
verbatim: Naval, siege, and cavalry prose. Flagged in the Mass Combat Guide's open gaps. No standard exists for any of the three.
notes: The origin statement of this docket item (restated in Pack Two); closed by Pack Three, Amendment Eight. Marked superseded for docket cleanliness, same basis as R2-OP-NAVAL_SIEGE_CAVALRY.

title: Practitioner POV during mass action, instinct is rarely
summary: A Stage XII practitioner inside a battle experiences none of the guide's constraints; the instinct is that this POV should be given rarely, since it dissolves the tension the framework exists to produce, but the call is Isaac's.
verbatim: Practitioner POV during a mass action. A Stage XII inside a battle experiences none of the constraints the guide is built on. My instinct is that this POV should be given rarely, because it dissolves the tension the entire framework exists to produce. Your call.
notes: The origin statement of this docket item (restated and narrowed in Pack Three, Amendment Nine, which rules before/after rather than "rarely"); see R3-9-PRACTITIONER_POV_RULING. Marked superseded for docket cleanliness, same basis as R2-OP-PRACTITIONER_POV_MASS_ACTION.

title: The removable-battle diagnostic
summary: If removing the battle would preserve the relationship change, the Act was not unrepeatable and the battle was decoration; rebuild the Act around something only the engagement made possible.
verbatim: If you can remove the battle and preserve the relationship change, the Act was not unrepeatable and the battle was decoration. Rebuild the Act around something the engagement made possible and nothing else could.

title: One Single Act per engagement, not the same pairing twice
summary: One Single Act per engagement — two dilutes both, three is a soap opera in armour; a campaign's several engagements should not all involve the same pairing, or the reader begins to expect the shape.
verbatim: One Single Act per engagement. Two dilutes both. Three is a soap opera in armour. A campaign arc may run several engagements and therefore several Acts, and they should not all involve the same pairing, because the reader will begin to expect the shape and expectation is what kills it.

title: The Single Act resolves in the aftermath, never by discussion
summary: The relationship change is legible in how the two characters handle an unrelated later scene; if a character ever says what the act meant, the amendment has been violated and the scene has been spent.
verbatim: In the aftermath, and not by discussion of the act itself. The relationship has changed and both parties behave differently. Neither raises it. The scene three days later is about a bucket, or a burial detail, or who takes which watch, and the change is legible in how they handle the bucket. If a character says what the act meant, the amendment has been violated and the scene has been spent.

title: The Single Act's four conditions
summary: The Single Act must be physical (a thing done with the body under load, not a decision or realisation), unrepeatable (the circumstance does not recur), witnessed but not discussed during the engagement, and ambiguous at the moment it happens to witness, reader and actor alike.
verbatim: It is physical. Not a decision, not a realisation, not a look held a beat too long. A thing done with the body under load.

title: A battle advances exactly one relationship, by one unrepeatable act
summary: A battle cannot hold six relationships the way a duel holds one; a battle advances exactly one relationship, and it advances it by a single unrepeatable act.
verbatim: The rule: a battle advances exactly one relationship, and it advances it by a single unrepeatable act.

title: The currency rule — Essence and time do not exchange
summary: A practitioner converts Essence into effect; an army converts time into ground; these do not exchange, so no technique holds ground — it may take, deny, break or unmake ground, never occupy it.
verbatim: A practitioner converts Essence into effect. An army converts time into ground. These do not exchange. Design consequence: no technique holds ground. A technique may take, deny, break or unmake ground and it may not occupy it. Any technique whose stated function is holding a position for a duration has been designed wrongly and should be rebuilt as a denial effect with a Sustain.

title: Domains break cohesion; the rout does the killing
summary: A seated Domain corrodes cohesion and the line breaks, with killing happening in the rout; assess a Domain-class technique by Re-form rather than by casualties.
verbatim: A seated Domain does not kill a formation. It corrodes cohesion, the line breaks, and the killing happens in the rout. Design consequence: assess any Domain-class technique by Re-form rather than by casualties. A Domain that kills sixty and does not break the line has failed.

title: Scaled techniques carry Frontage, Sustain and Re-form
summary: Any technique deployed against a formation carries Frontage, Sustain and Re-form alongside the standard seven fields, or it does not belong on a battlefield; counterplay is always exceeding Frontage, outlasting Sustain, or shortening Re-form.
verbatim: Any technique deployed against a formation carries all three fields in addition to the standard seven. A technique that cannot be given all three does not belong on a battlefield. Counterplay to any scaled technique is always one of three things: exceed its Frontage, outlast its Sustain, or shorten its Re-form.
notes: Restated from Pack One; check Pack One's own extraction for the original statement of these three fields once it is processed.

title: The magazine rule — a practitioner always knows what's left
summary: Essence is finite per practitioner per day and replenishes slower than expenditure under load; every technique's Cost field must be legible to the character using it, who never discovers mid-technique that they are empty.
verbatim: Essence is finite per practitioner per day, replenishment is slower than expenditure under load, and the practitioner always knows what they have left. Design consequence: every technique's Cost field must be legible to the character using it. A practitioner never discovers mid-technique that they are empty.

title: A practitioner is refilled by a Wellspring or not at all
summary: Essence cannot be shipped (it leaks in transit, needs an untransportable instrument to assay, dies with its owner); no consumable, technique or item may restore a practitioner's magazine.
verbatim: A practitioner is refilled by a Wellspring, or not at all. Essence cannot be shipped: it leaks in transit, cannot be assayed without an instrument that does not travel, and dies with its owner. Design consequence: no consumable restores a practitioner's magazine. Any technique, item or draft proposed to do so is refused at design.

title: Movement techniques are priced as expenditure, not mobility
summary: Speed is Essence; a character who arrives fast arrives depleted, and there is no free travel at Grade — a scene with one has spent a resource silently.
verbatim: High-Grade couriers give functional real-time command across a theatre. Speed is Essence, couriers are interdicted first, and formations trained on instantaneous command collapse harder when they lose it than formations that never had it. Design consequence: movement techniques are priced as expenditure, not as mobility. A character who arrives fast arrives depleted. There is no free travel at Grade and a scene that has one has spent a resource silently.

title: Voidic techniques are priced as artillery, not attack
summary: A Voidic practitioner is a poor attacker and the finest suppression instrument in the world; Voidic techniques are priced as artillery — slow to bring, slow to move, unable to defend themselves, needing a guard detachment, and affecting friendly output as readily as hostile.
verbatim: Aether Class VI devours where others emit. A Voidic practitioner is a poor attacker and the finest suppression instrument in the world, and those are the same fact. Design consequence: Voidic techniques are priced as artillery. Slow to bring, slow to move, cannot defend themselves, require a guard detachment, and affect friendly output as readily as hostile. A Voidic technique with a friendly-side exemption has been designed wrongly.

summary: Cozbi's combat grammar assignment was deferred by choice.
verbatim: Cozbi's combat grammar. Deferred by choice.

title: Cozbi Mahuo's canonical combat assignment
summary: Grammar Expenditure; signature move the Standing into the Ledger, not a bluff; answers plate with indifference; tells by crouching to examine rather than posturing, with speeded cadence signalling genuine alarm; status canonical, transcribed from the character card.
verbatim: | Grammar | Expenditure | | Signature | The Standing into the Ledger. He will do nothing for as long as it takes and this is not a bluff. | | Answer to plate | Indifference. He is not trying to get through it. | | Tell | Crouches to examine, never postures to threaten. Stress default is speed, so a Cozbi who has begun talking faster than his usual cadence has been genuinely alarmed and the reader should notice before the other characters do. | | Status | Canonical. Transcribed from the character card and the combat material, not invented. |

title: Writing Cozbi — refuse the spectacular exchange
summary: An Expenditure fighter is boring to write badly and terrifying to write correctly; refuse the temptation to give him a spectacular exchange — the scene should feel like the opponent is winning, repeatedly, at increasing cost, until the arithmetic arrives.
verbatim: Craft note for writing him: an Expenditure fighter is boring to write badly and terrifying to write correctly. The temptation is to give him a spectacular exchange. Refuse it. The scene should feel like the opponent is winning, repeatedly, at increasing cost, until the arithmetic arrives. Everything before the Ledger is the opponent succeeding.

title: Who fights in the Expenditure grammar
summary: Assigned to Cozbi, Legion summoners, construct-users, anyone operating through a conscripted lattice or projected vessel, and any fighter whose combat proposition is that the target of the blow is not the source of the working.
verbatim: Assign to: Cozbi, Legion summoners, construct-users, anyone operating through a conscripted lattice or a projected vessel, and any fighter whose combat proposition is that the target of the blow is not the source of the working.

title: The fourth grammar — Expenditure hunts cost
summary: Expenditure grammar does not seek to defeat the opponent; it makes the exchange asymmetric so everything the opponent does is expensive and everything the practitioner does is spent from somewhere else. Victory is arithmetic and arrives late.
verbatim: Expenditure grammar hunts cost. The practitioner does not seek to defeat the opponent. They seek to make the exchange asymmetric, so that everything the opponent does is expensive and everything they themselves do is spent from somewhere else. Victory is arithmetic and arrives late.
notes: The fourth combat grammar alongside Pack One's Blade, Verdict and Percussion; check for cross-references once Pack One is extracted.

title: The four Expenditure moves
summary: The Offering converts opponent capability into expenditure; the Standing converts time into advantage (only for a fighter who doesn't experience time as a resource); the Ledger converts the whole preceding engagement into one effect, un-repeatable per encounter; the Absence converts a victory into nothing by destroying the vessel while the practitioner is unaffected.
verbatim: | The Offering | Something expendable is put where the opponent must deal with it | Converts the opponent's capability into expenditure. The construct is not expected to win. It is expected to cost. |

title: The Expenditure tell and its two documented counterplays
summary: The tell is that the fighter is not looking at the opponent. Counterplay is reaching through the projection to the claims it carries (a Rescind-type working) or forcing a direct physical contest against the practitioner's own below-ceiling frame; both are documented as having worked once, neither is easy.
verbatim: Expenditure tell: the fighter is not looking at the opponent. In prose, have them looking at something adjacent, or crouching to examine something on the ground, which is Cozbi's documented posture and reads as either serene or obscene depending on what the reader already thinks of him. Counterplay, per canon: reach through the projection to the claims it carries, which has been done once and required a Rescind-type working. Or force a direct physical contest, which has also been done once and worked, because his own frame is genuinely below his ceiling.

title: Expenditure treats plate armour as irrelevant
summary: Plate is a cost problem rather than a defence problem to an Expenditure fighter, who is content to let armour do its job for as long as the wearer can afford to keep wearing it.
verbatim: Expenditure answers to plate: irrelevant. Plate is a cost problem rather than a defence problem, and an expenditure fighter is content to let armour do its job for as long as the wearer can afford to keep wearing it.

title: A charge is three seconds of decision and forty of consequence
summary: The decision (will the enemy line hold) is made at distance by both sides simultaneously; if it holds, the charge fails before contact, if it breaks, there is no contact at all, only pursuit.
verbatim: A charge is three seconds of decision and forty of consequence. The decision is whether the enemy line will hold, made at distance, by both sides simultaneously. If it holds, the charge fails before contact. If it breaks, there is no contact at all, only pursuit.

title: Cavalry is the only ordinary POV that carries the Field Register
summary: A cavalry POV is the only ordinary soldier who can carry the Field Register honestly, since the rider both sees and moves; use for orientation when needed, aware of the cost paid in intimacy.
verbatim: The rider sees, and the rider moves. They have both things the infantryman lacks, and the consequence is that a cavalry POV is the only ordinary soldier who can carry the Field Register honestly. Use them for orientation when you need it and be aware you are paying in intimacy.

title: The horse is a character with opinions
summary: The horse is frightened, tiring, can smell blood, and will not go where pointed if that is a hedge of spears; every good cavalry scene is partly about negotiating with an animal.
verbatim: The horse is a character with opinions. It is frightened, it is tiring, it can smell blood, it will not go where you point it if what you are pointing it at is a hedge of spears. Every good cavalry scene in the literature is partly about negotiating with an animal.

title: The pursuit is cavalry's real function, and it is not combat
summary: Per Section 6, pursuit is butchery of the unresisting from behind at a canter for as long as the horses last; the honest version does not let the cavalry POV enjoy it and does not let them refuse it either.
verbatim: The pursuit is the cavalry's real function and it is not combat. Per section 6, it is butchery of the unresisting from behind at a canter for as long as the horses last. Writing a cavalry POV means writing the person who does that work, and the honest version does not let them enjoy it and does not let them refuse it either.

title: Fire and water are the two naval deaths, not the blade
summary: Naval death is written as fire and water, not the blade.
verbatim: Fire and water are the two deaths. Not the blade. Write accordingly.

title: Motion is the naval sensory channel with no land equivalent
summary: Every physical action on a moving deck costs balance; fighting on a moving surface is closer to fighting drunk than to fighting on a slope and should be written that way.
verbatim: Motion is the second channel and has no land equivalent. The deck under a body that cannot plant. Every physical action costs balance. Fighting on a moving surface is closer to fighting drunk than to fighting on a slope and should be written that way.

title: The rout rule does not apply at sea
summary: A broken crew cannot run, so Section 6's rout rule does not apply; naval casualties concentrate in the fighting and the sinking rather than in a pursuit, making sea actions bloodier per engagement and rarer.
verbatim: The rout has nowhere to go. Section 6's central rule does not apply. A broken crew cannot run, so naval casualties concentrate in the fighting and in the sinking rather than in a pursuit. This is the single largest structural difference and it makes sea actions bloodier per engagement and rarer.

title: The naval sensory hierarchy inverts to sight-motion-sound-smell
summary: At sea the sensory order runs sight, motion, sound, smell (versus land's sound, pressure, smell, sight), because a ship gives a horizon and takes away footing.
verbatim: The sensory hierarchy inverts. Section 1's order (sound, pressure, smell, sight) was built for a man in a press. At sea it runs sight, motion, sound, smell, and the reason is that a ship gives you a horizon and takes away your footing.

title: Naval sight is rationed by capability, not visibility
summary: A sailor's Field Register is available continuously and is rationed by what the character can do about what they see, not by what they can see; write the helplessness of watching rather than the confusion of not seeing.
verbatim: Sight extends and becomes reliable. A sailor can see the whole engagement, which is the exact opposite of the infantryman's condition, and it changes the POV problem completely. The Field Register is available continuously and must therefore be rationed by a different instrument: not what the character can see, but what they can do about it. Write the helplessness of watching rather than the confusion of not seeing.

title: The Close Register is reserved for three tedium-breaks
summary: The Close Register is reserved for a sortie, a mine breaking through, and the storm; each arrives without warning and ends faster than the reader wants.
verbatim: The Close Register is reserved for the three things that break the tedium: a sortie, a mine breaking through, and the storm. Each should arrive without warning and end faster than the reader wants.

title: The disease is the siege's antagonist
summary: Per Walls and What Beats Them, the besieging camp gets the same sickness as the besieged at the same time and frequently loses more; the enemy in a siege scene is the ditch, and the garrison is scenery.
verbatim: The disease is the antagonist. Per Walls and What Beats Them, the besieging camp gets the same sickness as the besieged at the same time and frequently loses more. The enemy in a siege scene is the ditch, and the garrison is scenery.

title: Siege uses the Line Register by default
summary: A siege is experienced as a unit condition (camp, food, flux, digging progress) rather than personal action; weeks pass in the Line Register at a paragraph each, correctly.
verbatim: Use the Line Register as the default, not the Close. A siege is experienced as a unit condition rather than as personal action: the state of the camp, the state of the food, the state of the flux, whether the digging advanced today. Weeks pass in the Line Register at a paragraph each and this is correct.

title: The parley is the siege's climax, not the storm
summary: Everything a siege is about happens in the negotiation, because both commanders know what a storm means; write the parley as the climax and the storm, if it comes, as the failure of the actual drama.
verbatim: The parley is the scene. Everything a siege is about happens in the negotiation, because both commanders know what a storm means. Write the parley as the climax and the storm, if it comes, as the failure of the actual drama.

title: Siege tedium is written by specificity, not length
summary: One precisely observed repeated detail carries a month — the same gap in the wall, seen from the same place, on a different day, with something small changed.
verbatim: Tedium is written by specificity, not by length. One precisely observed repeated detail carries a month. The same gap in the wall, seen from the same place, on a different day, with something small changed.

title: What the practitioner POV covers before, after, and during
summary: Before covers the costing-out arithmetic and the decision what to spend and on whom; after covers what the practitioner looks at on a field they made and whether they can name anyone; during, use the soldier, with the practitioner appearing only as weather the POV soldier experiences and doesn't understand.
verbatim: - Before is where it belongs. The costing-out arithmetic, the decision about what to spend and on whom, the knowledge that the levy in front of them exists to be expensive. That is the most damning interiority available in the setting and it is wasted if it appears while they are fighting. - After is the second place. What a practitioner looks at on a field they made. Whether they can name anyone. - During, use the soldier. If the practitioner must appear, they appear as weather: something the POV soldier experiences and does not understand, arriving from outside the four-foot wedge.

title: The costed-out exception, spend it once
summary: The single exception to the practitioner-POV ruling: a practitioner who has been costed out inherits every section-1 constraint the moment their magazine empties, so a POV beginning able to see the whole battle and ending able to see twelve feet is the strongest use of the perspective available — spend it once.
verbatim: The single exception: a practitioner who has been costed out. The moment their magazine empties they inherit every constraint in section 1 at once, and a POV that begins with a person who can see the whole battle and ends with a person who can see twelve feet is the strongest use of the perspective available. Spend it once.

title: Practitioner POV is available before/after a mass action, closed during
summary: A high-Stage practitioner inside a battle experiences none of the constraints the guide is built on; handing the reader that POV mid-engagement dissolves the fog, pressure and helplessness every other section exists to construct, so the POV is open before and after an engagement and closed during it.
verbatim: A high-Stage practitioner inside a battle experiences none of the constraints this guide is built on. They can see. They are not in the press. They know what is happening. Handing the reader that POV during an engagement dissolves the fog, the pressure and the helplessness that every other section exists to construct. Ruling: the practitioner POV is available before and after an engagement and is closed during it.

title: The deletion test for a suspected gloss
summary: Delete the candidate sentence and read the passage; if it means the same thing, it was a gloss and stays deleted; if meaning is genuinely lost, the failure is in the line above and that line is rebuilt, never the gloss restored.
verbatim: Delete the candidate sentence. Read the passage without it. - The passage means the same thing. It was a gloss. It stays deleted. - The passage genuinely loses the meaning. The failure is in the line above, not the line below. Rebuild the original so it carries its own freight. Never restore the gloss.

title: Free indirect discourse is not gloss
summary: A sentence in the POV's own idiom that could be wrong and reveals the character interpreting is characterisation and is kept; a sentence in the narrator's neutral, authoritative register that reveals nothing about anybody's interior is cut.
verbatim: Free indirect discourse is not gloss, and this amendment must not be used to strip interiority. The test is whose vocabulary: - The sentence is in the POV character's idiom, could be wrong, and reveals the character doing the interpreting. Keep it. That is characterisation. Sodoku mis-reading a room is worth three paragraphs. - The sentence is in the narrator's neutral analytic register, is authoritative, and reveals nothing about anybody's interior. Cut it. That is the author explaining their own scene.

title: A gloss is a sentence that only states prior significance
summary: A gloss is any sentence whose only function is to state the significance of the sentence before it, disguised as texture or observant narration.
verbatim: Name it. A gloss is any sentence whose only function is to state the significance of the sentence before it.

title: The Third Recurrence rule for a loaded word
summary: A loaded word gets one physical response on first use and no comment; meaning arrives on the third appearance through change — another character uses it, the usual user withholds it, or register makes earlier uses retroactively legible. Withholding is the strongest of the three.
verbatim: A loaded word gets one physical response on first use and no comment at all. Meaning arrives on the third appearance, and it arrives through change: someone else uses the word, or the person who always uses it withholds it, or it lands in a register that makes the earlier uses retroactively legible. Withholding is the strongest of the three.

title: The three disguises of a gloss
summary: The etymological gloss explains why a character chose a word; the register gloss explains what a tone signified; the stakes gloss restates in abstract vocabulary an event the reader already watched concretely, usually at paragraph-end.
verbatim: The etymological gloss. The narrator explains why a character chose the word they chose.

title: Significance lives in three places, never in narration
summary: Significance may live in a physical tell adjacent to the line, in another character's bodily reaction, or in a governed callback — never in narration itself.
verbatim: Three places, and narration is not one of them. 1. A physical tell adjacent to the line. Hild's hand on the arm of the chair. Whether it opens or closes. 2. The other character's reaction. Somebody in the room hears the word and does something about it with their body. 3. A callback, governed by the rule below.

title: Zero glosses per scene, not rationed
summary: The gloss budget is zero per scene; there is no acceptable first instance.
verbatim: Zero glosses per scene. Not rationed. There is no acceptable first instance.

title: The approach ladder, decelerate into the hit
summary: Decelerate into the hit (long, then medium, then the landing) so the reader's eye slows as it arrives, then expand again afterward since consequence is cumulative and belongs in cumulative syntax.
verbatim: Decelerate into the hit. Long, then medium, then the landing, so the reader's eye is slowing as it arrives and the short sentence reads as a stop instead of one more item. Expand again afterwards: consequence is cumulative in fact and belongs in cumulative syntax, which is the register's proper home.

title: The chain ceiling, no more than two long sentences in a row
summary: No more than two consecutive sentences may run over 25 words; the third breaks, or the paragraph does.
verbatim: The chain ceiling. No more than two consecutive sentences over 25 words. The third breaks, or the paragraph does.

title: The clause cap at the beat
summary: Within the three sentences bracketing a value turn, no sentence carries more than one subordinate or coordinate clause.
verbatim: The clause cap at the beat. Within the three sentences bracketing a value turn, no sentence carries more than one subordinate or coordinate clause. A reversal delivered inside a chained sentence has been delivered at the same volume as the furniture.

title: The conjunction audit at a beat
summary: Count coordinators per sentence (and, as, while, which, because); two or more inside a beat-carrying sentence is a fail, though the same count outside a beat is style and left alone.
verbatim: Count coordinators per sentence: and, as, while, which, because. Two or more inside a sentence carrying a beat is a fail. Outside a beat it is style and left alone.

title: Hard ceilings on payoff sentences and paragraph shape
summary: A payoff sentence carries at most 10 words and zero subordinate clauses; at least 18% of a scene's sentences run under 8 words; and no paragraph closes on three consecutive sentences over 18 words.
verbatim: | Words in the payoff sentence | 10 | | Subordinate clauses in the payoff sentence | 0 | | Sentences under 8 words, share of scene | 18% floor | | Paragraphs closing on three consecutive sentences over 18 words | 0 |

title: The landing rule, the hit is the shortest sentence and sits last
summary: The emotional hit takes the shortest sentence in its paragraph and sits last; anything trailing it is the paragraph clearing its throat after the point.
verbatim: The landing rule. The emotional hit takes the shortest sentence in its paragraph and sits last. Anything trailing it is the paragraph clearing its throat after the point.

title: Sentence-length variance is enforced per paragraph
summary: Sentence-length variance is enforced at the paragraph level, not just the document level; the global CV stays as a floor and stops being sufficient on its own.
verbatim: Amended: variance is enforced per paragraph. The global CV stays as a floor and stops being sufficient.

title: The run rule, no three same-length sentences in a row
summary: No three consecutive sentences may fall within forty percent of each other's word count.
verbatim: The run rule. No three consecutive sentences within forty percent of each other's word count. Lengths of 22, 19 and 24 constitute a run, and a run is a flat stretch of road however good the individual sentences are.

title: Bodies are exempt from the reification budget
summary: Concrete nouns doing concrete things (hands shaking, a jaw setting, a tail going still) are not counted against the reification budget.
verbatim: Bodies are exempt. His hands shook. Her jaw set. The tail went still. Concrete nouns doing concrete things, not on this budget.

title: The Guild clerk test for the Licensed Class
summary: If the thing could appear as a line on a ledger, in a writ, or in a Bench finding, reify it freely; if it could not, it costs budget.
verbatim: The test: could a Guild clerk file it? If the thing could appear as a line on a ledger, in a writ, or in a Bench finding, reify it freely. If it could not, it costs budget.

title: Concrete first; an object in the room always wins
summary: Before reifying, check whether an object already in the room can carry the same freight; the object always wins.
verbatim: Concrete first. Before reifying, check whether an object already in the room can carry the same freight. The object always wins.

title: Reification is legal; density is the failure
summary: Reification is a genuine Hermetic-register instrument and any single instance reads well; the failure is density — ten good instances in a scene leave nothing solid for the reader to stand on.
verbatim: This is not a bad move and it will not be banned. It is a genuine Hermetic-register instrument, it belongs to the native tongue, and any single instance reads well. That is the problem exactly. The calibration section waves it through because it evaluates instances, and the failure is density.

title: The Licensed Class of abstractions that genuinely are objects
summary: A debt, claim, verdict, name, standing, bearing, holding, writ, seal, title, warrant, attribution or tally is a closed-class WOTR abstraction the world already treats as a thing that moves between hands; reifying these is description, not device, and is unbudgeted and free.
verbatim: A debt is a transferable instrument that can be declared never to have existed. A claim is carried. A verdict is issued and can be rescinded. A name, a standing, a bearing, a holding, a writ, a seal, a title, a warrant, an attribution, a tally: the Guild Accord, The Bearing and the Holding, Value, Coin and Trade and the Bench of Attribution all treat these as things that move between hands and can be seized, forged, voided or lost. Licensed instruments are unbudgeted and free.

title: Reification never delivers the beat
summary: Reification is atmosphere and a poor delivery vehicle for a turn; the value flips on a body or an object, never on a personified noun.
verbatim: Never at the beat. Reification is atmosphere and a poor delivery vehicle for a turn. The value flips on a body or an object, never on a personified noun.

title: One unlicensed reification per paragraph
summary: Two unlicensed reifications in a single paragraph produces a bogged-down feeling independent of the scene total.
verbatim: One per paragraph. Two unlicensed reifications in a single paragraph is the bogged-down feeling on its own, independent of the scene total.

title: One unlicensed reification per page in procedural scenes
summary: In procedural or ledger scenes, the unlicensed reification budget tightens to one per page, since the Licensed Class is already doing that work there and unlicensed instances would go invisible against it.
verbatim: One per page in procedural or ledger scenes. The licensed class is already doing this work there, and unlicensed instances go invisible against it.

title: Reification is an abstraction handled as a physical object
summary: Reification gives an abstract noun a physical verb, handled by characters as an object in the room; the tell is the verb, not the noun (hand, pass, set, carry, place, take, give, hold, put, return, offer, lift, drop, weigh, lay, arrive, land, sit, settle, drain).
verbatim: An abstract noun given a physical verb and handled by the characters as an object in the room. The silence sat between them. He handed her the governance of it. The arithmetic moved across his face. Permission changed hands.

title: Two unlicensed reifications per scene, different abstractions
summary: At most two unlicensed reifications per scene, of different abstractions; a third is a fail regardless of quality, and the same abstraction may be reified only once.
verbatim: Two per scene, different abstractions. The third is a fail regardless of quality. The same abstraction may be reified once — silence is handled once or the scene has a tic.

title: The reification watch-list nouns

summary: Fails any chain of 3+ sentences over 25 words, 4+ flat runs, a short-sentence share under 10% (warns under 18%), and reports every paragraph closing long-long-long.

title: Prose flesh derives from the Western tradition
summary: Prose register, humour, characterisation method, narration authority and tonal architecture derive from the Western tradition (Martin's POV discipline, Tolkien's cultural register and elegiac capacity, Abercrombie's dry brutality).
verbatim: The flesh changes. Prose register, humour, characterisation method, narration authority and tonal architecture now derive from the Western tradition: Martin's POV discipline, Tolkien's cultural register and elegiac capacity, Abercrombie's dry brutality.

title: The system lives in the Codex, never in prose texture
summary: The system is author-facing and document-facing — it lives in the Codex, character sheets, in-world treatises and technical-reveal beats; it does not live in prose texture, narrator commentary, or character affect.
verbatim: The operative consequence: the system is author-facing and document-facing. It lives in the Codex, the character sheets, the in-world treatises, and the technical-reveal beats where a mechanism earns explicit naming. It does not live in prose texture, narrator commentary, or character affect. A reader who never opens a codex should experience WOTR as a Western epic that happens to be unusually rigorous about what magic costs.

title: The Eastern mechanical skeleton stays exactly as it is
summary: WOTR runs an Eastern skeleton under Western flesh; the systematic density (Stages, Wellsprings, Bands/Grades/Coherence/eta, Codex glyph grammar, Family/Physics Domain, the character sheet, the Design Chain, EU costs) does not get diluted, softened, or made impressionistic.
verbatim: WOTR runs an Eastern skeleton under Western flesh. The skeleton stays exactly as it is. Sixteen Temperance Stages, sixty Wellsprings, Bands and Grades and Coherence and eta, the Master Codex glyph grammar, Family and Physics Domain assignment, the seventeen-section character sheet, Trigger through Counterplay, EU costs to the unit. That systematic density is a light-novel and xianxia inheritance and it is the correct engine for this project. It does not get diluted, softened, or made impressionistic. Section 3.3's division of hard and soft labour stands untouched.

title: Characterisation moves from declaration to inference
summary: A character is established by what they choose under pressure, what they refuse, what they notice first, and what others say about them when absent — not by being vividly themselves in every line; the reader assembles the person.
verbatim: Characterisation moves from declaration to inference. A character is no longer established by being vividly themselves in every line. They are established by what they choose under pressure, what they refuse, what they notice first in a room, and what other people say about them when they are not present. The reader assembles the person.

title: The Foil Function survives intact
summary: Deliberate moral and rhythmic contrast between paired characters (Merry/Pippin, Sam/Frodo, Tyrion/Bronn, Jaime/Brienne, Glokta/Severard) is Western-native and remains actively tracked.
verbatim: The Foil Function (Directive Sec. 3.8) survives intact. It was never Eastern.

title: The Manhwa Energy Directive is struck in full
summary: Personality vomiting, reaction shots as characterisation, loud opinions as a default register, bizarre/exaggerated minor NPCs, absurdist method alongside genuine stakes, humour as a tone exception, and escalation as a prose-level pacing register are no longer craft law and become active tells; escalation survives only as plot architecture (Scene Writing Process Guide §2).
verbatim: Struck in full from the project instructions and from Section 4's sanctioned-exception clause. The following are no longer craft law and should be treated as active tells if they appear in a draft.

title: Yoko-against-Sodoku survives as a foil, delivered without deadpan
summary: Yoko against Sodoku is a precision-versus-instinct foil, not a comedy routine; its humour now arrives through what Yoko declines to say, never a deadpan beat landing on a punchline.
verbatim: Yoko against Sodoku survives. The precision-versus-instinct dynamic is a foil, not a comedy routine. What changes is the delivery: the humour in it now arrives through what Yoko declines to say, never through a deadpan beat landing on a punchline.

title: Information is tracked per POV, not per reader
summary: Before a scene, name what this POV knows, what they wrongly believe, and what the reader knows that they do not.
verbatim: Information is tracked per POV, not per reader. Before a scene, name what this POV knows, what they wrongly believe, and what the reader knows that they do not.

title: The narration never winks at the reader
summary: No line acknowledges that the reader knows better than the POV.
verbatim: The narration never winks. No line acknowledging that the reader knows better.

title: A POV's wrong conclusion must be well-reasoned
summary: Irony built on a character being stupid is not irony; a POV must apply sound reasoning to a corrupted premise, not simply be foolish.
verbatim: The POV's wrong conclusion must be well-reasoned. Irony built on a character being stupid is not irony. Ned is not a fool; he is applying Northern law in a Southern court.
notes: Elevated to status:live: Pack Fifteen §4 (already ratified, live) explicitly confirms this instrument "stands," following the same precedent used for Pack Seven content Pack Twelve confirms survives.

title: Default to the POV who knows least about what is coming
summary: Where a scene could be written from two POVs, write it from whoever knows least about what is coming; a default, breakable with reason.
verbatim: Where a scene could be written from two POVs, write it from whoever knows least about what is coming. This is a default, breakable with reason.
notes: Elevated to status:live: Pack Fifteen §4 (already ratified, live) explicitly confirms this instrument "stands," following the same precedent used for Pack Seven content Pack Twelve confirms survives.

title: Elegy attaches to a named concrete thing that is gone
summary: Elegy attaches to a named concrete, specific thing that is gone (a road, a dye colour, a lost word, a dying craft), never to abstractions; grief for "the old world" is furniture.
verbatim: Elegy attaches to a named concrete thing that is gone. A road nobody maintains. A dye colour nobody can make since the salt corridor closed. A word that survives only in a formula whose meaning is lost. A craft with three living practitioners. Never to abstractions; grief for "the old world" is furniture.
notes: Elevated to status:live: Pack Fifteen §4 (already ratified, live) explicitly confirms this instrument "stands," following the same precedent used for Pack Seven content Pack Twelve confirms survives.

title: Elegy is delivered flat; the reader does the mourning
summary: Section 1.2's saga restraint governs elegy: state the loss and move on, without raising the prose's voice.
verbatim: Flat delivery. Section 1.2's saga restraint governs. State the loss and move on. The reader does the mourning.
notes: Elevated to status:live: Pack Fifteen §4 (already ratified, live) explicitly confirms this instrument "stands," following the same precedent used for Pack Seven content Pack Twelve confirms survives.

title: An elegiac loss is often irreversible and nobody's fault
summary: What distinguishes elegy from grimdark's systemic cruelty is that the loss is often irreversible and often nobody's fault; some things are simply taken, some simply end.
verbatim: The loss is often irreversible and often nobody's fault. This is what distinguishes elegy from grimdark's systemic cruelty, and WOTR needs both. Some things are taken. Some things simply end.
